lesson.title: Cell Eating: Phagocytosis and the Engulfment of Whole Particles
lesson.summary: Phagocytosis is the dramatic, large-scale form of endocytosis in which a cell physically wraps its membrane around an entire particle, such as a bacterium, and swallows it whole.
lesson.body:
The word phagocytosis comes directly from Greek roots meaning cell eating, and the name is a fairly literal description of what happens. Rather than the small, evenly sized vesicles typical of most endocytosis, phagocytosis begins when a cell detects a large particle nearby, often through specific surface receptors that recognize markers on the particle's surface, and responds by extending arm-like projections of cytoplasm called pseudopodia around it. These pseudopodia are driven by rapid, localized assembly of the actin cytoskeleton just beneath the plasma membrane, pushing the membrane outward on multiple sides until the projections meet on the far side of the particle and fuse together, fully enclosing it in a large vesicle called a phagosome.

Because the target of phagocytosis can be as large as an entire bacterial cell or a chunk of cellular debris, the resulting phagosome is correspondingly large compared to typical endocytic vesicles, and its formation consumes a substantial amount of the cell's actin and ATP in a short burst of activity. Once sealed off, the phagosome does not remain a passive container. It fuses with one or more lysosomes to form a phagolysosome, and the acidic, enzyme-rich environment inside the lysosome breaks the engulfed material down into its basic molecular components, which can then be recycled by the cell or, in the case of immune cells, used to generate fragments displayed on the cell surface to alert other parts of the immune system.

In animals, phagocytosis is central to innate immune defense. Macrophages and neutrophils, two types of white blood cells, patrol tissues and the bloodstream specifically to recognize and phagocytose invading bacteria, engulfing them whole and destroying them inside phagolysosomes, one of the body's first lines of defense against infection. Phagocytic cells also clear out dead or damaged cells and cellular debris throughout the body, a routine housekeeping role that is just as important as pathogen defense, since ninety percent of it happens without ever triggering the visible symptoms associated with fighting infection.

Phagocytosis is not unique to specialized immune cells, and its evolutionary origin has nothing to do with immunity at all. Single-celled protists such as Amoeba use essentially the same pseudopodia-driven mechanism purely to feed, engulfing smaller organisms or food particles suspended in their environment and digesting them in the resulting phagolysosome. Comparing the amoeba's feeding behavior with a macrophage's defensive behavior makes clear that phagocytosis is fundamentally a feeding and clearance mechanism that vertebrate immune systems later co-opted for defense, rather than something that evolved for immunity in the first place.

As one of the two major specialized forms of endocytosis, phagocytosis is defined by what it takes in and how it takes it in: large, discrete, particulate matter, brought in through an active, receptor-guided, actin-driven engulfment process. The next section turns to the other major form, pinocytosis, which handles a very different kind of cargo, dissolved solutes and fluid, using vesicles that are far smaller and formation that is often far less selective.
